passage:
"Harish, helmet!" Parul held it out at the gate.
"Didi, it's two minutes on the cycle to tuition."
"Two minutes is enough."
"It squashes my hair. Nobody wears one for short rides."
"Remember Sunny from B-block? Short ride too."
"Sunny was showing off. I ride properly."
"And the auto that took the turn without looking? Was Sunny showing off then?"
"Didi, relax. Nothing's going to happen to me."
"That's exactly what Sunny said."
Harish grinned and pushed off the kerb. "I'm different."
Parul didn't smile. She stood in front of the cycle, holding the helmet out, until he sighed, snatched it and jammed it on.

qa.q: Why does Harish say he doesn't need the helmet?
qa.a: He says it's two minutes on the cycle to tuition and the helmet squashes his hair.

qa.q: Why does Harish feel that nothing is going to happen to him?
qa.a: He tells himself Sunny was showing off and he rides properly, so harm feels like it belongs to others, while the comfort of no helmet is right now.

qa.q: Which of Parul's moves worked, and why?
qa.a: Standing calmly in front of the cycle worked better than more arguing, because it kept the choice in front of him and let him give in without a fight.

qa.q: What is it like for Parul to watch Harish push off without a helmet?
qa.a: Parul remembers what happened to Sunny, so she feels a real fear that he doesn't, which is why she didn't smile.

grounding: A teenager insists he won't get hurt riding without a helmet, seeing accidents as something for other riders.

passage: I'm Amandeep, and I'm writing this a few months after the thing with Jatin's vape. It started in Class 10, behind the school water tank. Jatin had a flavoured one, mango, and passed it around. I knew the posters in the corridor said it was harmful. But in my head those posters were about other people, adults who'd smoked for twenty years, not a sixteen-year-old taking a few puffs. The sweet taste and everyone laughing felt huge right then; 'later' felt like a made-up word. Within weeks Jatin was sneaking out between classes, and irritable when he couldn't. That scared me more than any poster. I stopped going to the water tank, and I told my older cousin, who helped Jatin talk to the school counsellor.

qa.q: Where did it start?
qa.a: It started in Class 10, behind the school water tank.

qa.q: Why didn't the corridor posters feel like they applied to Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep felt safe, thinking the posters were about other people who had smoked for years, and the sweet taste and laughter right then felt much bigger than 'later'.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do that was wise?
qa.a: Amandeep stepped away from the water tank and told an older cousin, who helped Jatin reach the school counsellor.

qa.q: How did Jatin's changes affect Amandeep?
qa.a: Seeing Jatin sneak out between classes and turn irritable scared Amandeep more than any poster, and made the harm real.

grounding: A teenager recalls believing vaping harms only other people, while the immediate buzz outweighed any thought of later.

passage:
Note from Coach Trisha, district swimming camp, day 4
This afternoon Ojas and two older boys slipped away to the old quarry pond behind the camp. There's a board there saying the water is deep and cold. When I found them, Ojas was on the ledge, ready to jump. He said, laughing, "Coach, I'm the strongest swimmer here. Those warnings are for people who can't swim." He seemed to truly believe it. The rush of the jump was all he could see.
I didn't shout. I sat with him on the bank and asked who he thought the board was written for. He shrugged. I told him strong swimmers get cramps in cold water too.
Next steps: told the camp head and called his parents this evening. Tomorrow the whole group walks to the quarry with the lifeguard to hear about the risks on site.

qa.q: What does the board at the quarry pond say?
qa.a: The board says the water is deep and cold.

qa.q: What does Ojas's laughing reply suggest about how he sees the danger?
qa.a: It suggests Ojas feels confident, even thrilled, truly believing the warning is for weaker swimmers, while the rush of the jump outweighs any thought of harm.

qa.q: How did Coach Trisha respond without lecturing?
qa.a: Coach Trisha sat with him, asked who the board was for, told the camp head and his parents the same day, and planned a site visit with the lifeguard.

qa.q: How might Ojas's parents feel when they hear about the quarry?
qa.a: They would likely feel scared, and grateful the coach found him in time.

grounding: A coach records a strong teenage swimmer believing a danger sign is only for weaker people, and the calm steps taken.

passage:
14 Aug
Went to the fair with Rajni didi and her cousin. On the way back I rode pillion on his scooter, no helmet because it was in the dickey and I didn't want to wait. The wind in my face at night, the lights on the canal road, honestly the BEST feeling.
Rajni didi said, "Jasleen, put the helmet on, silly girl." Please. Accidents happen to careless people who ride fast in traffic. We were only on the canal road, and her cousin drives well.
Also, everyone in my class says their brothers ride without one. Nothing ever happens to them.
When we reached home Rajni didi was really quiet. She told me her college friend fell off a scooter last year on a road just like that one. She didn't say more.
I still don't think it would happen to me. But I keep hearing how quiet she was.
Jasleen

qa.q: Where was the helmet when Jasleen rode pillion?
qa.a: It was in the dickey.

qa.q: Why did riding without a helmet feel safe to Jasleen?
qa.a: The wind and lights felt so good in the moment, and she believed accidents happen only to careless people riding fast in traffic, not to her on the canal road.

qa.q: What could Rajni didi try next time to help Jasleen choose the helmet?
qa.a: She could ask Jasleen to wait the few seconds and hand her the helmet before they start, and talk calmly about her friend so it doesn't feel like a scolding.

qa.q: What is it like for Rajni didi to hear Jasleen shrug off the helmet?
qa.a: For Rajni didi it may bring back the fear of her college friend's fall, which is why she went quiet instead of arguing.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows her riding without a helmet, believing harm happens to others, drawn by the thrill of the ride in the moment.

passage: Every morning Lalremsiami raced her bicycle down the steepest road in Aizawl to school, no helmet, hair flying, overtaking taxis on the bends. The school counsellor, Nazia ma'am, called her in after a teacher saw her skid at the gate. "You know Lalrina from Class 11 broke his collarbone on that road?" "He's reckless," Lalremsiami said. "I know what I'm doing. Nothing's going to happen to me." Nazia ma'am didn't lecture. She drew two circles on a page: "the rush now" and "what could happen later." "At your age the brain makes the first circle feel huge and the second feel far away. That's normal. It's also why we plan ahead." Lalremsiami looked at the circles. "Fine. What if I wear a helmet on the steep bit?" "Every bit," said Nazia ma'am, and handed her one from the sports room.

qa.q: What happened to Lalrina on that road?
qa.a: He broke his collarbone.

qa.q: Why does Lalremsiami believe nothing will happen to her?
qa.a: She feels thrilled and invincible on the fast ride, so injuries seem to belong to reckless others, not to someone who knows what she's doing.

qa.q: How did Nazia ma'am respond, and why did it work?
qa.a: She explained without lecturing how the brain makes the rush feel bigger than the risk at this age, then gave a practical step: a helmet for every ride.

qa.q: How might Nazia ma'am feel about the offer to wear a helmet on the steep bit?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and encouraged, but firm enough to ask for the helmet on every bit of the ride.

grounding: A teenage girl rides downhill without a helmet believing harm is for others, and a counsellor explains the pull of the rush and hands her a helmet.

passage:
Noor,
Don't start. I know you think vaping is dangerous. But it's only at weekends, and the stuff about lungs is for people who do it all day, not for me. I play football, I'm fit, I'll quit whenever I want. Honestly the only bad part was Papa finding the vape in my jacket yesterday. He didn't shout, which was worse. He just sat down and said we're going to meet the school counsellor together on Monday. He said something about my age, how the brain is wired to chase the good feeling now and push the later stuff away. I rolled my eyes. But I did look it up last night, and some of it was about people exactly like me.
Vaibhav

qa.q: When is Vaibhav meeting the school counsellor?
qa.a: On Monday, together with Papa.

qa.q: Why does Vaibhav believe vaping won't cause harm?
qa.a: Vaibhav feels fit, confident and in control, so the harms seem to belong to other people who do it all day.

qa.q: What is wise about Papa's response?
qa.a: He stayed calm, explained how the brain at this age chases the good feeling now, and arranged to see the school counsellor together.

qa.q: How might Noor feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Noor might feel worried but a little hopeful, noticing that Vaibhav looked it up and saw it described people like Vaibhav.

grounding: A teenager writes that vaping's harms are for other people, while a parent responds calmly and arranges a counsellor visit.

passage: Gurpreet, you asked why I stopped going to the canal. Okay. You know how in the monsoon everyone jumps from the old bridge? I did it every Sunday. People kept saying the current is strong after rain, a boy drowned there two years ago, all that. I honestly thought, that's other people. Kavitha is a good swimmer; nothing happens to me. Then last month the water was brown and fast and I jumped anyway. The current pulled me under the second arch. I came up, I don't even know how, and a fisherman dragged me to the bank. I walked home soaked and told Mummy everything that same evening. She held me for a long time, then went with me to the panchayat office to ask for a warning board. It's there now.

qa.q: Who dragged Kavitha to the bank?
qa.a: A fisherman.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha keep jumping even after hearing about the drowning?
qa.a: Kavitha felt confident and thrilled, believing danger was for other people and a good swimmer was safe.

qa.q: What did Kavitha and Mummy do after the near miss?
qa.a: Kavitha told Mummy everything that evening, and they went together to the panchayat office to ask for a warning board.

qa.q: What might Mummy have felt hearing the story?
qa.a: Mummy was probably terrified and deeply relieved, holding Kavitha for a long time before acting to protect others.

grounding: A teenager explains believing river danger was for others until a near miss, and the same-day family response that followed.

passage:
Week 1, Monday. Ojas cycled to tuition on the highway service road without his helmet. "Helmets are for slow people," he told Swati at the gate. "Accidents happen to bad riders." The helmet hung on the hook at home.
Week 2, Thursday. A boy from the next batch came to tuition with his arm in a sling. He had been clipped by an auto at the same turn Ojas took every day. He had been a good rider too, everyone said. Ojas didn't say anything, but he rode home slower.
Week 3, Tuesday. Swati noticed the blue helmet on Ojas's head. "Changed your mind?" He shrugged. "My mother saw the boy's photo in the parents' group. She made me promise." A pause. "And I kept thinking, he also thought it wouldn't be him."

qa.q: What happened to the boy from the next batch?
qa.a: He had been clipped by an auto at the same turn Ojas took every day and came with his arm in a sling.

qa.q: Why did Ojas believe he didn't need a helmet in week 1?
qa.a: He felt confident and invulnerable, sure that accidents only happen to bad or slow riders.

qa.q: What helped Ojas change, and what could help other teenagers?
qa.a: Seeing that a good rider was hurt at his own turn, and his mother's promise; seeing real cases close to home and a parent setting a clear rule can help others.

qa.q: How might Swati see the change in Ojas?
qa.a: Swati seems relieved and a bit surprised, noticing he now takes the risk seriously.

grounding: Shows over weeks a teenager who rides without a helmet believing accidents happen to others, until a real case close to home changes his mind.

passage: Lalit, you think those boys racing bikes on the canal road are heroes? Sit, let your Rashmi Bua tell you about Meerut, when I was fifteen. My friends and I used to jump into the canal from the old bridge in July, when the water was high. Everyone said a boy had drowned there once. We laughed. That was a weak swimmer, we said. Not us. I jumped maybe twenty times that summer. Then one afternoon the current pulled me under the bridge. My friend's elder brother, who was fishing, pulled me out by my plait. I coughed water for an hour. At home my mother didn't shout. She just held me and went, that same evening, to tell the other girls' mothers. After that the bridge had a guard every monsoon. We weren't braver than that boy. We were just luckier, until I wasn't.

qa.q: Where did Rashmi Bua and her friends jump into the canal?
qa.a: From the old bridge.

qa.q: Why did young Rashmi laugh at the story of the boy who drowned?
qa.a: She felt fearless and sure it only happened to weak swimmers, not to her and her friends.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed what happened at the bridge?
qa.a: Her mother going that same evening to tell the other girls' mothers, which led to a guard at the bridge every monsoon.

qa.q: How was the friend's elder brother affected that afternoon?
qa.a: He had to act fast to pull a drowning girl out, a frightening moment that showed the danger was real.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling as a teenager that the dangers of jumping into a canal were only for others, until she was nearly swept away.

passage: It was the night before the physics practical, rain drumming on the tin roof of the bus shelter where Jatin and Urmila were waiting. A boy from their class pulled out a small vape and passed it around. "It's just flavoured air," he said. Jatin reached for it. Urmila frowned. "You know the counsellor said it's still harmful." Jatin laughed. "That's for people who do it every day. I'm not going to get hooked. That happens to other people." The bus was twenty minutes late and the rain wasn't stopping. Urmila said quietly, "My cousin said that exactly. Now he can't get through the morning without it." Jatin paused, the vape halfway to his mouth. Then he handed it back. The next day Urmila walked with him to the counsellor's room, and he asked the questions he'd been too proud to ask.

qa.q: What did the boy say the vape was?
qa.a: It's just flavoured air.

qa.q: Why did Jatin think he would not get hooked?
qa.a: He felt confident and invulnerable, sure that harm happens to people who use it every day, not to him.

qa.q: What small step helped Jatin, and what could other teens try?
qa.a: Urmila's honest story about her cousin and going with him to the counsellor next day; others can ask a counsellor or trusted adult instead of trusting "not me".

qa.q: How might Urmila feel when Jatin hands the vape back?
qa.a: Urmila probably feels relieved and glad her quiet story about her cousin got through to him.

grounding: Shows a teenager believing the harm from vaping happens only to others, until a friend's real story and a counsellor help him think again.

passage:
In Aizawl, the hill roads are steep and wet most of the year. Lalremsiami, sixteen, had started riding her cousin's scooter to tuition without a helmet. "It's only five minutes," she told her uncle Jagdish when he saw her.

"Five minutes is enough," he said.

"Nothing will happen. I'm careful."

On Thursday, a car came round the bend too fast. Lalremsiami braked hard, skidded, and stopped inches from the drain. Her knee was scraped. Her head was fine, but only by luck.

That evening Jagdish sat with her on the steps. He didn't shout. "Everyone your age feels like nothing bad will happen. Your brain is built to think the ride matters more than the risk. That's normal. But the road doesn't care how careful you are."

Her hands were still shaking. She nodded.

The next morning, he left his old helmet on her scooter seat. She wore it.

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami stop after skidding?
qa.a: Inches from the drain.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami believe nothing would happen without a helmet?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt confident and safe, believing that being careful meant accidents happen to other people.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do after the skid, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Jagdish talked calmly instead of shouting, explained why teens feel invincible, and left her a helmet the next morning.

qa.q: How did Jagdish seem to feel when he first saw her riding without a helmet?
qa.a: Jagdish seemed worried, warning her that five minutes is enough for an accident.

grounding: A teenager rides a scooter without a helmet believing harm is for others, until a near miss and a calm uncle.

"Parveen didi! Why are you in my bag?"

"It's nothing. Everyone does it."

"It's not nothing."

"It's not like cigarettes. It won't hurt me."

"Everyone. And I only do it sometimes. I'm not going to get hooked."

passage:
I'm Ira. Last year, my friend Naveen and I rode his bike to the lake almost every evening. Neither of us wore helmets. We thought helmets were for old people and bad riders.

Naveen's mum used to say, "One day something will happen." We laughed. Nothing ever happened to us.

Then one evening in March, a dog ran across the road. Naveen swerved. We both fell. I scraped my arms. Naveen hit his head on the kerb.

He was okay, eventually. A few stitches, a week at home. But the doctor said a helmet would have saved him from most of it.

I kept thinking: we were so sure it wouldn't be us. It always felt like other people's story.

Now I wear a helmet every time, even for five minutes. And when my younger cousin says, "I'm careful, I'll be fine," I tell her about the dog.

qa.q: What ran across the road?
qa.a: A dog ran across the road.

qa.q: Why did Ira and Naveen not wear helmets?
qa.a: They felt overconfident and safe, sure accidents only happened to old people and bad riders, not to them.

qa.q: What does Ira do now, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Ira wears a helmet every time and tells the younger cousin about the dog, turning the lesson into protection for others.

qa.q: How might Naveen's mum have felt after the accident?
qa.a: Naveen's mum was probably frightened and upset, having warned them many times.

grounding: A teenager recalls riding without a helmet believing harm was for others, until a friend was hurt in a fall.

passage:
Coach's note, monsoon term, week 6
Jeevan arrived at practice again today on his cycle with no helmet, hair dripping, having come along the highway stretch where the trucks spray water. When I asked, he grinned: "Accidents happen to people who can't ride. I'm fast." Hafsa, who wears her helmet every day, said a boy from her lane fell on that stretch last month. Jeevan shrugged: "He must've been careless." He honestly seems to believe it can't be him; the thrill of racing the school bus matters far more to him right now than anything that might happen later. I didn't lecture. I called his mother that evening, and we agreed he rides only with the helmet the school lends and takes the service lane. I'll check at the gate each morning this week.

qa.q: Which road does Jeevan ride on to reach practice?
qa.a: The highway stretch where the trucks spray water.

qa.q: Why does Jeevan feel safe riding without a helmet?
qa.a: He feels confident and invulnerable, believing accidents happen to people who can't ride, and the thrill of racing the bus matters more to him right now.

qa.q: Which step in the coach's response is most useful, and why?
qa.a: Calling his mother and agreeing on the school helmet and the service lane, with checks at the gate, because it protects him now instead of relying on a lecture.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel hearing Jeevan's answer?
qa.a: Hafsa may feel worried and frustrated, since she knows a boy from her lane fell there and Jeevan waves it away.
